author_response_spans.text: **Response** : We thank this reviewer’s comments. Furthermore, we have addressed this reviewer’s concerns as detailed below and in the revised manuscript.
## Please see specific comments below:
## 1 _-Electron microscopy of caveolae:_

_The authors have now included EM analyses of caveolae as requested, and report that caveolae are increased in number in aibp2 KO zebrafish and that recombinant AIBP reduces the number of caveolae. Caveolae are morphologically defined as flask-shaped 50-80 nm invaginations of the plasma membrane. The authors should therefore remove the data and quantifications of “atypical” morphological structures that they name caveolae, such as “open caveolae” in Fig. 2d. These may not represent caveolae at all and in any case, their content is not altered in aibp2 KO fish. The atypical ”small size caveolae” in Fig. 5a should also be left out for the same reason_ .

_Regarding the localization of APEX2-tagged VEGFR3 (WT or AAA-mutant) in caveolae, the DAB reaction (dark precipitate) can identify the localization of the signal but is not quantitative. This is because the extent of the DAB reaction and its potential saturation are not well controllable. I would recommend leaving the quantifications in panel 4f out and only present the exemplary images to demonstrate the caveolar localization of VEGFR3. However, considering that the AAAmutant is expressed at similar levels as the WT receptor (panel 4d), the question now arises where the mutant receptor is localized, if not in caveolae_ .
## **Response** : Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback.

As suggested, we have removed the data and quantifications related to “open caveolae” in Fig. 2d and “small size caveolae” in Fig. 5a. The revised data continue to support our conclusion that caveolar abundance is increased in the absence of Aibp2.

Regarding the APEX2-tagged VEGFR3 analysis, we agree that the DAB signal is not suitable for quantitative assessment due to potential variability in the reaction. Accordingly, we have removed the quantification in Fig. 4f and now present representative images to illustrate the caveolar localization of VEGFR3.

As shown below, VEGFR3[AAA] predominantly localizes intracellularly (white dotted line in the middle panel indicates the cell boundary), consistent with its reduced presence in caveolae despite similar expression levels to the wild-type receptor (scale bar: 20 μm). Elucidating the

mechanism underlying this localization pattern and how it increases VEGFR3 signaling will require further investigation and falls beyond the scope of this manuscript.
## 2- _APOA1 expression:_

_In the revised manuscript, the authors have included elegant data on WT and mutant APOA1 tagged with a photoconvertible protein, to track APOA1 dynamics in zebrafish and to demonstrate that WT APOA1 rescues but an APOA1 mutant reported to be defective in ABCG1-dependent HDL efflux does not rescue the thoracic duct lymphatic defect in aibp2 KO zebrafish. They coin the APOA1 mutant deltaC58 and cite ref. 71. This paper does not have such a mutant - but rather APOA1delta185-243. Apparently, the authors decided to rename a C-terminal deletion of 58 amino acids as deltaC58. If this is the case, it should be clearly spelled out._

**Response** : Thank you for pointing this out. To improve clarity and conserve space in the revised manuscript, we referred to apoA-IΔ[185–243], as described in this publication[1] , as APOA1[ΔC58] .
We have clarified this nomenclature in the manuscript to avoid any confusion.

3- _Determination of cholesterol efflux, caveolin-enriched domains and cholesterol content: The sterol efflux data are based on a fluorescent sterol analog, not on measuring the efflux of cholesterol. This should be clearly mentioned in the results and the conclusions toned down accordingly. The efflux of fluorescent sterols typically differs considerably from that of cholesterol. E.g. Fig. 3 title “Cholesterol efflux potentiates VEGFR3 signaling” is misleading as cholesterol efflux is not measured. In Fig. 3 e-f, CT and H+A is not defined._

_Membrane cholesterol availability is measured indirectly by a FACS-based analysis of D4 binding and is therefore not a measure of “the free cholesterol levels”, as claimed. D4 binding measures the plasma membrane accessible pool of cholesterol that is not in complex with sphingomyelin. This should be more clearly spelled out in the results._

**Response** : Thank you for pointing this out. We agree that the cholesterol efflux assay in hLECs utilizes a fluorescent BODIPY-cholesterol rather than directly measuring free cholesterol. Notably, this assay has shown a significant correlation (~80%) with [³H]-cholesterol-based efflux measurements[2] and has been applied in clinical studies[3] . In our current study, we also quantified cholesterol content in isolated caveolar fractions and observed a reduction following AIBP treatment—a finding consistent with AIBP-facilitated cholesterol efflux.

In addition, our previous work using [³H]-cholesterol in human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) demonstrated that AIBP enhances cholesterol efflux[4] , a finding independently validated by others (Fig. 1D in ref[5] ). HUVECs have also been used as an in vitro model to investigate molecular mechanisms underlying lymphangiogenesis[6] .

While we acknowledge the limitations of using a fluorescent BODIPY-cholesterol, the combination of fluorophore-tagged cholesterol efflux assays, caveolar cholesterol quantification, and our prior radiolabeled studies provides a coherent and compelling body of evidence supporting the role of AIBP in promoting cholesterol efflux in LECs. In response to your comments, we have revised the Results section and moderated the conclusions accordingly as: “Supporting the role of AIBP in caveolae regulation, incubation of hLECs with recombinant AIBP increased _fluorescent BODIPY-_ cholesterol efflux to HDL (Extended Data Fig. 4b), _measured using a surrogate non-radioactive assay for [³H]-cholesterol efflux[2, 3]_ ”. (Italicized text indicates revised content.)

We have updated the title of Fig. 3 to “Cholesterol regulates VEGFR3 signaling” to more accurately reflect the data. In Fig. 3h, we have clarified the labeling by changing ‘CT’ to ‘Ctrl (control)’ and ‘H+A’ to ‘HDL+AIBP’.

We now specify that D4-EGFP binding reflects the accessible pool of plasma membrane cholesterol not complexed with sphingomyelin, rather than total free cholesterol levels. The revised sentence reads: “As anticipated, the _accessible_ free cholesterol levels of _lyve1[+]_ ECs in _apoa1bp2[-/- ]_ embryos were reduced by overexpression of wild-type APOA1 but not APOA1[∆][C58] (Extended Data Fig. 5f and g), as illustrated by FACS-based analysis of D4-GFP staining, a GFP fusion protein of perfringolysin O that _binds the pool of plasma membrane-accessible cholesterol not complexed with sphingomyelin_ .” (Italicized text indicates revised content.)
## 4- _Lymphangiogenesis rescue experiments with atorvastatin:_

_The atorvastatin rescue of LEC specification in aibp2 KO mutants may have off-target effects beyond cholesterol depletion. Atorvastatin at a dose of 1uM was used to show an increase in LECs, however it is known at nanomolar concentrations that atorvastatin displays toxicity during_
_zebrafish development, with reported effects on intracranial haemorrhage, ciliogenesis and muscle development. As such, these data are not informative and could be removed_ .

**Response** : Thank you for the thoughtful feedback. While atorvastatin at 1 μM rescued LEC specification in aibp2 KO mutants, we cannot exclude the possibility that its side effects on other tissues[7] may indirectly influence lymphatic fate. In light of this concern, we have removed this dataset from the revised manuscript as suggested.
## 5- _AIBP in human samples:_

_The data on human samples (Fig. 7c-d) are not convincing. While the antibody has now been described as their home-made antibody and a previous study using it for immunohistochemistry is cited (ref 30), a very minor (about 10%) reduction in the staining intensity of immunohistochemical samples cannot be considered reliable. Furthermore, there is no negative control such as preincubation of the antibody with the immunogen prior to immunostaining, the NL and LY samples have not been specified, nor is it explained how NL and LY are connected to each other. These data and the speculation that the AIBP-CAV1 pathway predisposes individuals to lymphatic deficiency should be removed_ .

**Response** : Thank you for the constructive feedback. NL (normal lymphatics) refers to normal skin tissue, whereas LY (lymphedematous) denotes lymphedematous tissue biopsied from the same patients. We did not include an antigen preincubation control because, based on our prior experience, preincubation of this antibody with antigen resulted in abnormally high background staining. We agree that the observed ~10% change is modest. While this antibody has been previously validated (see data below), we recognize that such a mild difference warrants further validation using an independent antibody.

## APOA1 binding protein promotes lymphatic cell fate and lymphangiogenesis by relieving caveolae-mediated inhibition of VEGFR3 signaling 

Received: 7 February 2025 Accepted: 28 May 2025 Check for updates 

Jun-dae Kim[1,2,3,13] , Surbhi Chaudhary[1,3,13] , Weiqing Chen 3,4,5, Jonathan Astin 6, Philip S. Crosier6, Pengchun Yu7, John P. Cooke 1,2,3,5, Henry J. Pownall 1,3,5,8, Hugo J. Bellen 9, Nhat-Tu Le1,3,5, Daniel L. Kiss2,3, Guangyu Wang 3,4,5, Stanley G. Rockson 10, Hong Chen 11 & Longhou Fang 1,3,5,12 

The lymphatic system maintains tissue fluid balance, and its dysfunction can result in lymphedema. Although cholesterol is essential for cellular function, its role in lymphatic development has remained unknown. Here, we identify APOA1 binding protein (AIBP) as a key regulator that promotes lymphatic endothelial cell fate specification and lymphangiogenesis. Mechanistically, AIBP reduces plasma membrane cholesterol content, thereby enhancing — VEGFR3 signaling by disrupting caveolae small plasma membrane invagina— tions formed by the scaffolding protein caveolin-1 (CAV-1) and relieving CAV– 1 mediated inhibition. In zebrafish and mice, AIBP loss impairs VEGFR3 signaling and lymphatic development, defects that can be rescued by CAV-1 deletion or by a VEGFR3 mutant (VEGFR3[AAA] ) lacking CAV-1 binding. Administration of recombinant AIBP augments VEGFC-induced lymphangiogenesis and accelerates the resolution of secondary lymphedema in adult – mice. These findings define the AIBP CAV-1 axis as a regulator of VEGFR3 signaling and lymphatic growth, offering potential therapeutic opportunities for treating lymphatic dysfunction.

The lymphatic vasculature is essential for maintaining interstitial fluid homeostasis, dietary lipid transport and immune surveillance[1][–][4] . A lymphatic contribution is implicated in the pathogenesis of a variety of diseases, including lymphedema, tumor metastasis, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, obesity, and diabetic mellitus[5][–][12] . Therapeutic augmentation of lymphangiogenesis has been documented to improve lymphatic structure and function[1][–][3][,][8][,][9] . Earlier studies show that the lymphatic system is derived from the embryonic cardinal vein, where lymphatic endothelial cell (LEC) progenitors are specified and subsequently migrate and establish the lymphatic network[1][–][3][,][13][,][14] . Recent studies indicate that a subset of lymphatics can be developed 

through non-canonical mechanisms[15][–][20] . During murine development, the assembly of the lymphatic vascular network is initiated at approximately embryonic day 9.5 (E9.5)[21] under the control of VEGFC signaling through its cognate receptor VEGFR3[22][,][23] . LEC fate commitment occurs through SOX18-induced expression of PROX-1, which, in concert with the orphan nuclear factor NR2F2 (also known as COUPTFII), dictates LEC differentiation from the cardinal vein[24][,][25] . In addition, GATA2, HHEX, and PROX1 itself have recently been shown to upregulate PROX1 expression[26][–][29] . The newly specified LECs subsequently bud from the cardinal vein and migrate (E10.0-E11.5) in a dorsolateral fashion to form lymph sacs and, thereby establish the functional

lymphatic vessels. VEGFC-induced VEGFR3 signaling is the major driver of lymphangiogenesis in vertebrates. Interestingly, in addition to the regulation of LEC sprouting, VEGFR3 signaling also controls LEC progenitor homeostasis by maintaining PROX1 expression levels in a positive feedback loop[22] . In zebrafish, Vegfc/Vegfr3 signaling increases Prox1[+] LEC progenitors in the axis vasculature[30][,][31] . Conversely, zebrafish or mice deficient in either CCBE1 (a critical matrix protein regulating VEGFC bioavailability), VEGFC, or VEGFR3 reduce PROX1positive LECs in the cardinal vein[23][,][32][–][34] . 

The developmental venous origin of the lymphatic endothelium and the requirement for VEGFC/VEGFR3 signaling in lymphangiogenesis are highly conserved from zebrafish to mice to humans[21][,][35] . In zebrafish, from 30 to 32 hours post fertilization (hpf), bi-potential precursor cells in the posterior cardinal veins (PCV) express Prox1 and undergo a Vegfc/Vegfr3-dependent cell division to generate lymphatic and venous daughter cells. In response to the Vegfc cue, the daughter cells on the PCV progressively acquire the LEC fate at 36 hpf; among these LECs, approximately half form parachordal LECs at the horizontal myoseptum by 48 hpf[31][,][34] . These parachordal LECs subsequently migrate ventrally and dorsally along the arterial intersegmental vessels (ISVs) at ~60 hpf[34] , to form the thoracic duct (TD), intersegmental lymphatic vessels, and dorsal longitudinal lymphatic vessels[21] . Wnt5b has been reported to function upstream of Prox1 to regulate proper lymphatic specification[16] .

Nevertheless, the role of cholesterol in LEC fate determination and lymphangiogenesis remains to be understood. 

Cholesterol is enriched in the endothelial caveolae, the 50–100 nm invaginations of the plasma membrane. CAV-1, the structural protein organizing the formation of caveolae, binds cholesterol directly and form these flask-shaped microdomains, which provide a platform to cluster and facilitate membrane-anchored receptor signaling[36][,][37] . CAV-1 ablation in mice eliminates caveolae[38][,][39] . Both the expression of CAV-1 and the formation of caveolae are dependent on cellular cholesterol levels[40][–][43] . In many cases, CAV-1 deficiency alters plasma membrane receptor signaling competence through disruption of caveolae[44][–][46] . How caveolae regulates lymphangiogenesis is unexplored. 

We have demonstrated that the secreted protein AIBP limits angiogenesis in a non-cell autonomous fashion. Mechanistically, extracellular AIBP binds to plasma membrane of endothelial cells, accelerates cholesterol efflux from endothelial cells to high-density lipoprotein (HDL) and reduces lipid raft/caveolae abundance, which in turn disrupts VEGFR2 signaling, thereby restricting angiogenesis[47][,][48] . Lymphatic vessels are structurally and functionally related to blood vessels. Many genes that are required for angiogenesis, such as VEGFR3, FGF, DLL4-NOTCH, angiopoietin-TIE2, Ephrin B2, and TGFβ family member ALK1, EPSIN and others, also function in lymphangiogenesis[5][,][49][–][59] . Thus, we sought to identify the role AIBPregulated cholesterol metabolism in lymphangiogenesis. In contrast to its suppressive role in angiogenesis, our studies reveal an unexpected role of AIBP in promoting lymphangiogenesis.

Mechanistically, AIBP augments VEGFC-engaged VEFGR3 signaling in a CAV-1-dependent fashion. Our findings provide potential therapeutic targets for the treatment of lymphatic disease. 

## Results 

## AIBP controls LEC lineage specification in zebrafish and from mESC 

−/−/−− 

To examine the role of Aibp2 in lymphangiogenesis, apoa1bp2 −/−/−− zebrafish were crossbred with fli1a:egfp zebrafish that express EGFP in the both the lymphatic and blood ECs[34][,][60] , generating apoa1bp2[−][/][−] ; fli1a:egfp. We performed immunostaining of Prox1 at 4 days postfertilization (dpf) because Prox1 is the master transcription factor that dictates LEC fate specification and is used to demarcate LECs[28][,][30][,][31] . In control siblings, ~4.3 of Prox1[+] LECs per seven segments were found in 

the TD. By contrast, Aibp2 knockout reduced the number of LECs to ~2.8 (Fig. 1a, b). The TD is the first functionallymphatic vessel formed in the zebrafish trunk, situated between the dorsal aorta (DA) and PCV. - Consistent with this, TD conduit formation is impaired in Aibp2 defi cient zebrafish at 4 dpf (Supplementary Fig. 1a, b). The LEC-associated genes were also downregulated in the ECs isolated from apoa1bp2[−][/][−] zebrafish compared with control animals (Supplementary Fig. 1c, d). These data suggest that Aibp2 regulates lymphangiogenesis. In contrast, Aibp2 knockout accelerated intersegmental vessel (ISV) growth – and sprouting (Supplementary Fig. 1e g). However, AIBP knockout had no effect on the formation of central artery (CtA) and sub-intestinal – vein (SIV) (Supplementary Fig. 1h k). Consistent with our prior reports, Vegfr2 activation was increased but Notch signaling was reduced in the Aibp2 deficient zebrafish (Supplementary Fig. 1l, m).

We next determined whether AIBP regulates lymphatic cell fate using the mESC to LEC differentiation model. Mouse embryoid bodies prepared from mESCs can be differentiated into derivatives of ectodermal, mesodermal, and endodermal tissues and recapitulate certain developmental processes[61][,][62] . We prepared mouse embryoid bodies and assessed LEC generation in a differentiation medium containing BMP4 and bFGF, followed by additional supplements on day 3 through day 7 with recombinant VEGFA and VEGFC in combination or with AIBP alone (Fig. 1c). From day 0 onwards during differentiation, LECs were identified by the expression of PECAM1, LYVE1, and PROX1, as previously reported[62][,][63] . Compared with control cells, VEGFA and VEGFC co-treatment increased the mRNA levels of the LEC-associated genes Prox1, Pecam1, and Lyve1, at day 5 and day 7 of differentiation (Fig. 1d). AIBP also substantially increased LEC specification as evidenced by robust expression of the LEC markers (Fig. 1d), comparable to the effect of VEGFA/C co-administration. A greater percentage of PECAM[+] / LYVE1[+] LEC population was detected by FACS analysis at day 7 of LEC differentiation in the presence of AIBP or VEGFA/C (Supplementary Fig. 2a, b). During LEC differentiation, our protocol also generated mesoderm and endoderm[62] , resulting in significant upregulation of genes encoding Vegfc and Adamts3, the latter proteolytically processing VEGFC to promote its maturation (Fig. 1e). These findings are consistent with the endogenous source of VEGFC observed in zebrafish[64][,][65] . These results suggest that AIBP regulation of LEC fate is conserved across evolution. 

We then investigated the pathways transmitting AIBP effect on LEC specification.

VEGFR3 and NOTCH1 are the critical regulators of lymphangiogenesis[3][,][12][,][49][,][66][,][67] . Because AIBP also regulates NOTCH signaling[47] , we queried whether NOTCH or VEGFR3 mediated AIBP effect on LEC specification. VEGFR3 inhibition using its specific inhibitor SAR13165 or knockdown using siRNA negated the effect of AIBP on promoting LEC specification, but NOTCH inhibitor DAPT had no effect (Fig. 1f and Supplementary Fig. 3a–f). The inhibitor effects and siRNA-mediated knockdown of VEGFR3 were validated (Supplemen– tary Fig. 3g i). The data suggest that AIBP promotes LEC fate through VEGFR3 signaling. 

We further isolated caveolae fractions from human lymphatic endothelial cells (hLECs) following AIBP treatment using sucrose gradient ultracentrifugation. As expected, AIBP reduced the protein abundance of VEGFR3 and CAV1 in caveolae (Supplementary Fig. 4a and Supplementary Table I). Among the significantly changed plasma membrane receptors, VEGFR3 is the key regulator of LEC fate and lymphangiogenesis (Supplementary Table II). Supporting the role of AIBP in caveolae regulation, incubation of hLECs with recombinant AIBP increased fluorescent BODIPY-cholesterol efflux to HDL (Supplementary Fig. 4b), measured using a surrogate non-radioactive assay for [³H]-cholesterol efflux[68][,][69] . Corroborating our cholesterol efflux analysis, AIBP treatment significantly reduced cholesterol levels in the caveolar fraction (~25% reduction, Supplementary Fig. 4c). Thus, our unbiased proteomic studies also validate VEGFR3 as the plasma membrane receptor mediating the AIBP function in LECs.

## Aibp2-mediated cholesterol regulation is essential for proper lymphangiogenesis 

Given that AIBP lowers plasma membrane cholesterol in hLECs (Supplementary Fig. 4c), we postulated that this reduces the levels of caveolae, a microdomain that is enriched with cholesterol. The presence of caveolae can be analyzed using transmission electron microscopy (TEM). In line with the reduction in plasma membrane cholesterol, AIBP 

treatment reduced the number of caveolae on hLEC plasma membrane (4.0 vs. 1.5/µm of cell edge, Fig. 2a, b)[70] . Conversely, loss of Aibp2 in zebrafish elevated caveolae abundance in the cardinal vein ECs compared with control animals (1.6 vs. 2.4/µm of cell edge, Fig. 2c, d). Our data demonstrate that AIBP controls caveolae abundance.

Since recombinant AIBP treatment reduced caveolae abundance (Fig. 2a, b), we postulated that this reduction was linked to enhanced VEGFR3 signaling. ## Recombinant AIBP administration promotes adult lymphangiogenesis in mice 

We further investigated the role of AIBP-CAV1 axis in adult lymphatic growth using the murine model. The corneas of adult mice lack lymphatic vasculature[85][,][86] , and is a widely used model to study injury or growth factor-induced lymphangiogenesis (Fig. 6a). We implanted VEGFC-containing pellets into the corneas of B6 mice, either alone or in combination with recombinant AIBP, APOA1 (the core protein component of HDL), or the CAV-1-modulating peptide (CAV-1 scaffolding domain, CSD). We used APOA1 in this assay due to technical difficulties in preparing HDL pellets. As expected, VEGFC pellet implantation elicited robust lymphangiogenesis (Fig. 6b). AIBP and APOA1 in combination or CSD further increased VEGFC-induced lymphangiogenesis (Fig. 6b, c). AIBP in combination with VEGFC exhibited a similar extent of pro-lymphangiogenic efficacy as AIBP and APOA1 combination (Fig. 6b, c). This is likely because mice generally exhibit high HDL levels resulting from APOA1 lipidation. In contrast, APOA1 and VEGFC combination did not show additive effects on lymphangiogenesis compared with VEGFC alone (Supplementary Fig. 15a, b). In addition, no prolymphangiogenic effect was detected with AIBP/APOA1 or CSD treatment in the absence of VEGFC (Supplementary Fig. 15c–f). These data suggest that the enhancement effect of AIBP or CAV-1 on corneal lymphangiogenesis is dependent on VEGFC.

Inflammation, mirrored by greater inflammatory cell infiltration, has been reported to influence corneal lymphangiogenesis in injuryinduced lymphangiogenesis[87][,][88] . We thus investigated the presence of leukocytes and macrophages in VEGFC-induced corneal lymphangiogenesis model. Immunostaining with CD45 and F4/80 antibodies followed by confocal microscopy reveals comparable numbers of corneal leukocytes and macrophages following by control PBS or VEGFC pellet implantation (Supplementary Fig. 16a–d). Therefore, the AIBP-CAV-1 axis regulation of lymphatics is unlikely to be dependent on inflammation. In addition, AIBP is reported to be anti-inflammatory in both the peripheral and central nerve system[78][,][89][,][90] , which argues against the possibility that AIBP facilitates lymphangiogenesis via an inflammation-dependent mechanism. Collectively, these data highlight the conserved role of AIBP-CAV1 axis in increasing lymphangiogenesis.

## Opposing roles of AIBP in angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis 

Our previous studies found that AIBP regulates both VEGFR2 and NOTCH1 signaling in angiogenesis and hematopoiesis[47][,][94] . Here, we show that AIBP increases lymphangiogenesis and instructs LEC progenitor specification, an event that is dependent on VEGFR3 signaling but not on NOTCH1 activity. Although LECs are derived from blood ECs, their functions and molecular identifications differ.

The fundamental differences between blood ECs and LECs may contribute to the distinct effects of AIBP on angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. While both VEGFR2/VEGFR3 and VEGFR3/VEGFR3 dimers function in lymphangiogenesis[95] , AIBP preferentially regulates VEGFR3 homodimers. Importantly, Vegfr3 per se, but not Vegfr2/Vegfr3 signaling is essential for TD lymphatic development in zebrafish[30][,][96] . 

It is not unprecedent that one protein may have the opposing effects on angiogenesis and lymphangiogenesis. For instance, RhoB 

ablation augments lymphangiogenesis but impairs angiogenesis in the cutaneous wound healing model[97] . Although NOTCH signaling limits angiogenesis[98][–][100] , NOTCH can inhibit or augment lymphangiogenesis in a context-dependent fashion[49][,][50][,][67][,][101] . ## Conserved role of AIBP in the regulation of LEC fate and lymphangiogenesis 

In the mESC-to-LEC differentiation model, we found that recombinant AIBP incubation displays a comparable effect as VEGFA/C combination on the LEC specification arising from mesodermal origin. Given that AIBP alone has no observable effect on VEGFR3 phosphorylation, this AIBP effect on LEC fate commitment is likely due to a synergistic effect of AIBP and increased VEGFC levels in the induced mesoderm/ endoderm[105][,][106] .

Furthermore, our siRNA-mediated VEGFR3 knockdown and inhibitor-based VEGFR3 inhibition compellingly demonstrate that AIBP controls LEC fate via VEGFR3.

## LC-MS/MS analysis 

An aliquot of the tryptic digest (in 2% acetonitrile/0.1% formic acid in water) was analyzed by LC-MS/MS on an Orbitrap Fusion[TM] Tribrid[TM] mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher Scientific), interfaced with a Dionex UltiMate 3000 Binary RSLCnano System. Peptides were separated onto an analytical C18 column (100 μm ID x 25 cm, 5 μm, 18 Å) at a flow rate of 350 nl/min. Gradient conditions were: 3%–22% solvent B for – – 40 min; 22% 35% solvent B for 10 min; 35% 90% solvent B for 10 min; 90% B held for 10 min (solvent B, 0.1% formic acid in acetonitrile). The peptides were analyzed using the data-dependent acquisition method, and the Orbitrap Fusion was operated to measure FTMS1 at a resolution of 120,000 FWHM, with a scan range of 350–1500 m/z, an AGC target of 2E5, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. During a maximum cycle time of 3 s, the ITMS2 spectra were collected in rapid scan rate mode, featuring HCD NCE 34, a 1.6 m/z isolation window, an AGC target of 1E4, a maximum injection time of 35 ms, and dynamic exclusion set for 20 s. 

## MS data acquisition 

The raw data files were processed using ThermoFisher Scientific’s Proteome Discoverer™ software, version 1.4. The spectra were searched against the Uniprot-Homo sapiens database using Sequest. The search results were refined to a 1% FDR for strict conditions and 5% for relaxed conditions using Percolator. For the trypsin analysis, up to two missed cleavages were allowed. The MS tolerance was set at 10 ppm, and the MS/MS tolerance was set at 0.8 Da.

## Statistics and reproducibility 

Statistical comparisons between two groups were performed using two-tailed Student’s t-tests with Welch’s correction. For comparisons involving multiple groups, one-way ANOVA was used, while two-way ANOVA was applied to assess multiple groups under different treatment conditions, followed by appropriate post hoc corrections. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. 

The substantial personnel turnover during the extended course of this study enhanced the reproducibility of the findings, as most experiments, if not all, were independently repeated by different researchers. No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. The experiments were not randomized.

The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment.

## (Remarks to the Author)

The extensively revised version the manuscript by the group of Longhou Fang and coauthors on the role of AIBP-CAV1VEGFR3 axis on lymphatic cell fate and lymphangiogenesis addresses many of the caveats previously raised, but also introduces additional concerns.

Overall, the manuscript is now quite convoluted and long. The number of models investigated is breathtaking but some of the experiments are insufficiently controlled or not stringent enough, and the writing is in several parts inaccurate or misleading. The text should be scrutinized throughout for clarity and accuracy of presentation. To streamline the manuscript, those parts that are too preliminary and not critical for the main message should be omitted.
Please see specific comments below:
## 1-Electron microscopy of caveolae:

The authors have now included EM analyses of caveolae as requested, and report that caveolae are increased in number in aibp2 KO zebrafish and that recombinant AIBP reduces the number of caveolae. Caveolae are morphologically defined as flask-shaped 50-80 nm invaginations of the plasma membrane. The authors should therefore remove the data and quantifications of “atypical” morphological structures that they name caveolae, such as “open caveolae” in Fig. 2d. These may not represent caveolae at all and in any case, their content is not altered in aibp2 KO fish. The atypical ”small size caveolae” in Fig. 5a should also be left out for the same reason.

Regarding the localization of APEX2-tagged VEGFR3 (WT or AAA-mutant) in caveolae, the DAB reaction (dark precipitate) can identify the localization of the signal but is not quantitative. This is because the extent of the DAB reaction and its potential saturation are not well controllable. I would recommend leaving the quantifications in panel 4f out and only present the exemplary images to demonstrate the caveolar localization of VEGFR3. However, considering that the AAA-mutant is expressed at similar levels as the WT receptor (panel 4d), the question now arises where the mutant receptor is localized, if not in caveolae.
## 2-APOA1 expression:

In the revised manuscript, the authors have included elegant data on WT and mutant APOA1 tagged with a photoconvertible protein, to track APOA1 dynamics in zebrafish and to demonstrate that WT APOA1 rescues but an APOA1 mutant reported to be defective in ABCG1-dependent HDL efflux does not rescue the thoracic duct lymphatic defect in aibp2 KO zebrafish. They coin the APOA1 mutant deltaC58 and cite ref. 71. This paper does not have such a mutant - but rather APOA1delta185-243. Apparently, the authors decided to rename a C-terminal deletion of 58 amino acids as deltaC58. If this is the case, it should be clearly spelled out.
## 3-Determination of cholesterol efflux, caveolin-enriched domains and cholesterol content:
The sterol efflux data are based on a fluorescent sterol analog, not on measuring the efflux of cholesterol. This should be

clearly mentioned in the results and the conclusions toned down accordingly. The efflux of fluorescent sterols typically differs considerably from that of cholesterol. E.g. Fig. 3 title “Cholesterol efflux potentiates VEGFR3 signaling” is misleading as cholesterol efflux is not measured. In Fig. 3 e-f, CT and H+A is not defined.

Membrane cholesterol availability is measured indirectly by a FACS-based analysis of D4 binding and is therefore not a measure of “the free cholesterol levels”, as claimed. D4 binding measures the plasma membrane accessible pool of cholesterol that is not in complex with sphingomyelin. This should be more clearly spelled out in the results.
## 4-Lymphangiogenesis rescue experiments with atorvastatin:

The atorvastatin rescue of LEC specification in aibp2 KO mutants may have off-target effects beyond cholesterol depletion. Atorvastatin at a dose of 1uM was used to show an increase in LECs, however it is known at nanomolar concentrations that atorvastatin displays toxicity during zebrafish development, with reported effects on intracranial haemorrhage, ciliogenesis and muscle development. As such, these data are not informative and could be removed.
## 5-AIBP in human samples:

The data on human samples (Fig. 7c-d) are not convincing. While the antibody has now been described as their home-made antibody and a previous study using it for immunohistochemistry is cited (ref 30), a very minor (about 10%) reduction in the staining intensity of immunohistochemical samples cannot be considered reliable. Furthermore, there is no negative control such as preincubation of the antibody with the immunogen prior to immunostaining, the NL and LY samples have not been specified, nor is it explained how NL and LY are connected to each other. These data and the speculation that the AIBPCAV1 pathway predisposes individuals to lymphatic deficiency should be removed.
## Reviewer #2
## (Remarks to the Author)

The authors have provided a comprehensive revision that includes extensive new data and analysis. They have addressed all of the major concerns that this reviewer previously raised. The study represents a very large body of work that is now well controlled and convincing. It demonstrates an exciting new mechanism controlling VEGFR3 signalling, lymphatic fate and lymphangiogenesis. I have no further suggestions of concerns.
I congratulate the authors on an impressive study that will be of broad interest to the field.
## Reviewer #3
## (Remarks to the Author)
The authors have done a lot of additional work, and they have succeeded in answering convincingly and very professionally all my questions and concerns.
On my part, I recommend the manuscript for publication in Nature Communications.

## (Remarks to the Author)

The authors have satisfactorily addressed all of my remaining concerns and I am happy to recommend publication of this impressive study. Please note the apparent typo in the Abstract (AIBP, by reducing plasma membrane - not plasma - cholesterol...)
